articles.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
articles.summary: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
articles.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
articles.titleTr: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
articles.summaryTr: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
articles.articleText: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged - Published In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day. A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable. "Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC. "Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up." Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed. Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding. In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district. Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village. "As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC. He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school. "They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled. After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain. "This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do." A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people. While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat. These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding. "Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda. "If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us." The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested. The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it. The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires. But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets. "We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference. He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved. Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones. "If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said. - 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted - Published11 November - A really simple guide to climate change - Published6 November Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more. The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn. Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024. Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa. Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation. But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience? "If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam. "Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited." Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support. "The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued. She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience. "When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa. "Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable." African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support. "Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency. "But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document." The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action. Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles. "It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said. But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it. "Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said. Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures. In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out. UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense. But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions. Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes. "We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said. "My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too." articles.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
articles.summary: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
articles.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
articles.titleTr: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
articles.summaryTr: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
articles.articleText: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say - Published European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv. "Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic". They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing. Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks. Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One. In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part. Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks". "That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine." But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans". Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable". Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition. Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions. Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no." The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine". "These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz. He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen. - Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance - Published7 hours ago "A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945. He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity." "The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be." Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks. The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato. There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table. But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine. It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory. As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage. And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved. He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge. Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not. articles.articleTextTr: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say - Published European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv. "Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic". They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing. Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks. Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One. In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part. Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks". "That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine." But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans". Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable". Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition. Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions. Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no." The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine". "These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz. He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen. - Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance - Published7 hours ago "A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945. He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity." "The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be." Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks. The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato. There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table. But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine. It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory. As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage. And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved. He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge. Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not. "I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches. Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply. - Published7 hours ago

articles.titleTr: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
articles.summaryTr: Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary is among the big investors looking to Canada as a data centre development destination, while his US project faces local opposition.
articles.articleText: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back - Published As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity. "Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections. While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects. Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids. "Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview. "The question really is whether or not we want to go for that." Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences. At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built. The western Canadian province, rich with natural gas deposits, has pitched itself as "North America's destination of choice" for AI data centres, including by offering a "concierge" service for investors to help build these projects at "unparalleled speed". One of those investors is Kevin O'Leary, the Canadian businessman, TV personality and an ally of Donald Trump, who announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres - one in Alberta and one in the US state of Utah. His planned sites, both named Wonder Valley, are being received in very different ways on either side of the border. Residents in Utah have organised a fierce opposition campaign., external The pushback led outgoing state senator Stuart Adams to demand in June that O'Leary scale down the project by 75%, external, from 40,000 to 13,000 acres. Financing for the Utah Wonder Valley data centre is still underway, and it is unclear when - and if - shovels will hit the ground on the project. The proposed 7,000-acre, 7.5-gigawatt Alberta Wonder Valley project, meanwhile, has received strong backing from both the provincial government and the local municipality. The project is billed as "off-grid", external, relying on its own power system fuelled by natural gas sourced from the region. In April, the Alberta government exempted the project from an environmental impact assessment, external, arguing it was unnecessary, though it will still need to obtain permits prior to construction. The project was met with only limited opposition at a local town hall earlier this year. One resident, Dan Harms, told Bloomberg in June , externalthat he saw the economic benefits of the Wonder Valley data centre and that it was being built "out in the middle of nowhere". In an interview with BBC News, Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf, of Greenview Municipality in north-western Alberta, said the project was the "perfect fit" for his rural community, which had been looking for an industrial tenant to fill a resource-rich parcel of land for 13 years. Some community members have expressed concern about the amount of water needed to cool the proposed site annually, which is projected to be six million cubic metres, or about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size swimming pools. Ratzlaf argued the amount was a drop compared to the annual flow of the nearby Smoky River, from which the centre would pull water. More broadly, he said he believed that economic benefits to the region outweighed potential risks. "It's a giant warehouse with computer equipment inside," he said, arguing that it was less risky than petrochemical plants that could have been built in its place. Speaking to BBC News, the CEO overseeing both O'Leary projects, Paul Palandjian, said the two were proceeding at an "equal" pace. He acknowledged it had become more of a "hot topic" in the US than in Alberta. But there are signs public anger towards AI data centres in Alberta has grown in recent months. Recent public information sessions on provincial AI data centre plans were attended by some furious residents. "If no one wants this, why are you pushing forward with this?" one resident asked in an August town hall reported on by the Canadian Press, external, held shortly after Alberta announced that Meta would build a C$13bn ($9bn; £6.8bn) AI data centre in the province. Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has also recently sued the government over its decision to override the environmental assessment for O'Leary's Wonder Valley data centre, labelling it "irrational" in court filings. This week, the Alberta government proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built in a bid to ease some concerns. There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country. On Saturday, hundreds of protesters gathered in Canada's Atlantic province of Nova Scotia against a proposed AI data centre, external that will be used by technology giant Anthropic. But experts say the US backlash offers a cautionary tale for Canada as it tries to capitalise on the AI boom. "AI is generally not very popular. This is both true in Canada and the United States," noted Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on the national sovereign AI compute strategy. "I think we could experience some of the same backlashes if we're not thoughtful about it," he said. So far, lawmakers in Canada have stood firm. The Carney government, which has made reducing Canada's reliance on the US a priority, has framed the development of AI data centres as a matter of national security and sovereignty. It has projected that Canada needs to expand its computing capacity 16-fold over the next four years to meet domestic demand. Alberta is defending its data centre plans by saying they will create jobs and generate revenue, and that sites will be developed "responsibly". In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford has said that his province needs to move "full steam ahead" with building data centres. Mullin said one reason the backlash had been less severe in Canada was simply due to scope and timing. "There has been less of these projects happening, and as a result, they've attracted less attention," he said. Canada has released some high-level guidance on data centre development, which has been co-signed by Anthropic, Meta and other big AI players. It calls on data centres to pay for electricity costs, minimise water use and create long-term benefits for the regions they are in. If politicians don't tread carefully, Bek MacIntosh, an Alberta resident who has fought a proposed hyperscale data centre in her community, said she believed public discontent could translate into angry votes, like those seen in the US. MacIntosh successfully halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta,, external over concerns with its scale, scope and proximity to her home. Even after her eight-month battle, she said she was not opposed to all AI infrastructure and believed Canada had the resources and landscape to build them responsibly. But she fears Alberta has opened the door to "the most reckless of reckless developers", and warned that voters might have a "knee-jerk reaction" if provinces don't take care to develop AI data centres responsibly. "And I don't think any political party in Canada is prepared for it." Related topics - Published11 November - Published6 November - Published6 November

articles.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
articles.summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.

articles.titleTr: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
articles.summaryTr: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.
articles.articleText: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC - Published In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie. "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life." Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war. Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million. Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege. They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling. On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon. From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below. Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August. Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers. "Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz. "It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous." She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors. "I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says. War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen. Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa. More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes. In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones. A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability. In Taiz, it is a threat to survival. An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that. Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died. The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him." Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas. They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply. He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe". If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards. "Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan. It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us. "The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents." He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says. On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally. He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do. The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid. That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations. What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan. He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance. "Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages". Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win. How long can the city hold out, I ask. "Until the population perishes," he replies. Many in Taiz are resisting. They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own. They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line. Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight. Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way. When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then. Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum. He tells us this fight is different to 2015. "This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves." He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children. But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism". The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union. "They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city." But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest. "Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes." The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us." Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it. But could they fight their way in? Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does. "Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says. His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war. Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away. "I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party." As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community. "Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports." articles.articleTextTr: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC - Published In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie. "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life." Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war. Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million. Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege. They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling. On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon. From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below. Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August. Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers. "Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz. "It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous." She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors. "I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says. War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen. Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa. More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes. In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones. A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability. In Taiz, it is a threat to survival. An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that. Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died. The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him." Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas. They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply. He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe". If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards. "Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan. It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us. "The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents." He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says. On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally. He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do. The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid. That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations. What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan. He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance. "Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages". Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win. How long can the city hold out, I ask. "Until the population perishes," he replies. Many in Taiz are resisting. They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own. They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line. Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight. Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way. When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then. Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum. He tells us this fight is different to 2015. "This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves." He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children. But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism". The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union. "They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city." But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest. "Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes." The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us." Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it. But could they fight their way in? Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does. "Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says. articles.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
articles.summary: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.
articles.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
articles.titleTr: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
articles.summaryTr: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.
articles.articleText: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force - Published New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force. Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason. Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all". But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers. The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed. Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities. Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said. Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it. If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks". Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients. But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests. Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party. There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden. Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers. The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. "We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said. The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees. Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.

articles.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of the lunch break
articles.summary: What is acceptable to eat at your desk, without annoying your colleagues?
articles.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
articles.titleTr: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of the lunch break
articles.summaryTr: What is acceptable to eat at your desk, without annoying your colleagues?
articles.articleText: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of the lunch break - Published There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's. Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish. From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive. "We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah. She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left". 'Suss out the smelliness' Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed". He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk. But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc". "The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk". Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them. "In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy – I swear by a good boiled egg." She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten." Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick". "I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues. "Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette." Do you take a lunch break? While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place. In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other. A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so. However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk. "While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR. "Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health." Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity". "I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says. But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time". His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it". "Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says. Related topics - Published15 December 2025 - Published30 January

articles.title: Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet to leave after nine years at company
articles.summary: Guillemet helped establish Ledger’s Donjon security lab and says his departure has been planned for months.
articles.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
articles.titleTr: Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet to leave after nine years at company
articles.summaryTr: Guillemet helped establish Ledger’s Donjon security lab and says his departure has been planned for months.
articles.articleText: Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet to leave after nine years at company Guillemet helped establish Ledger’s Donjon security lab and says his departure has been planned for months. Ledger chief technology officer Charles Guillemet announced he will be leaving the company at the end of 2026, after nine years at the company. In a post on LinkedIn on Thursday, Guillemet said he joined as chief security officer in December 2017, around three years after Ledger was founded. He launched Ledger Donjon, the company’s attack lab, a year later. “We’ve been preparing this transition for many months, so Ledger’s teams, partners and roadmaps are ready. I’m bullish on Ledger’s future,” said Guillemet. Guillemet has been a central figure in Ledger’s security operations, first as chief security officer and later as chief technology officer. He helped establish the Ledger Donjon attack lab, which tests hardware and software vulnerabilities. According to Guillemet, Ledger devices now secure roughly 20% of the world’s crypto assets. “The threat landscape changed too. AI is making attacks cheaper, faster and easier to scale,” he added. “The question we spent a decade answering for crypto (how do you protect what matters when any device can be compromised?) is now a question for every company, every AI agent and every government.” Guillemet did not disclose details of his next venture but said he was “building something new” and would “dedicate my time to solving this security mess.” Guillemet’s announcement comes weeks after Ledger disclosed that attackers had modified genuine hardware wallets with hidden components designed to capture users’ recovery phrases, and slipped the devices into authorized resellers. The tampering cases were initially reported in Asia, with subsequent incidents identified in Europe and the United Arab Emirates. He helped establish the Ledger Donjon attack lab, which tests hardware and software vulnerabilities. According to Guillemet, Ledger devices now secure roughly 20% of the world’s crypto assets. “The threat landscape changed too. AI is making attacks cheaper, faster and easier to scale,” he added. “The question we spent a decade answering for crypto (how do you protect what matters when any device can be compromised?) is now a question for every company, every AI agent and every government.” Guillemet did not disclose details of his next venture but said he was “building something new” and would “dedicate my time to solving this security mess.” Guillemet’s announcement comes weeks after Ledger disclosed that attackers had modified genuine hardware wallets with hidden components designed to capture users’ recovery phrases, and slipped the devices into authorized resellers. The tampering cases were initially reported in Asia, with subsequent incidents identified in Europe and the United Arab Emirates. articles.titleTr: Denizcilik ve havacılıkta gümrük muafiyeti değişti! Yeni kurallar devreye alındı
articles.summaryTr: Ticaret Bakanlığı, deniz ve hava ulaştırmacılığında kullanılan işletme ve donatım malzemelerinin gümrük muafiyeti uygulamalarını yeniden düzenledi. Muafiyet kodları ve GTİP bazlı eşya tanımlamaları güncellenirken teknik düzenlemeler BİLGE sistemine aktarıldı.
articles.articleText: Denizcilik ve havacılıkta gümrük muafiyeti değişti! Yeni kurallar devreye alındı - Ticaret Bakanlığı, deniz ve hava ulaştırmacılığında kullanılan işletme ve donatım malzemelerinin gümrük muafiyeti uygulamalarını yeniden düzenledi. Muafiyet kodları ve GTİP bazlı eşya tanımlamaları güncellenirken teknik düzenlemeler BİLGE sistemine aktarıldı. Ticaret Bakanlığı, denizcilik ve havacılık sektörlerinde kullanılan işletme ve donatım malzemelerine yönelik gümrük muafiyeti uygulamalarını değiştirdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanlığı ile ortak yürütülen çalışmalar kapsamında hazırlanan yeni genelgeyle, 4458 sayılı Gümrük Kanunu ve ilgili mevzuat çerçevesindeki uygulamalar güncellendi. Düzenlemenin, sektör temsilcilerinin sahadaki ihtiyaçları ve talepleri dikkate alınarak hazırlandığı bildirildi. Gümrük muafiyet kodları yeniden düzenlendi Yeni düzenlemeyle havacılık ve denizcilik sektörlerinde gerçekleştirilen gümrük işlemlerinde kullanılacak muafiyet kodları yeniden belirlendi. Kodların düzenlenmesinde sektör, eşya ve yetkilendirilmiş yararlanıcı kriterleri dikkate alındı. Böylece hangi eşyanın hangi koşullarda muafiyet kapsamında değerlendirileceğine ilişkin uygulamaların standartlaştırılması hedeflendi. Denizcilikte de GTİP bazlı sisteme geçildi Düzenlemenin öne çıkan başlıklarından biri de denizcilik sektöründe kullanılan donatım ve işletme malzemelerinin sınıflandırılması oldu. Denizcilikte kullanılan bu malzemeler, havacılık sektöründe olduğu gibi Gümrük Tarife İstatistik Pozisyonu (GTİP) bazında belirlendi. Bu adımla eşya tanımlamalarında ve gümrük işlemlerinde standartlaşma sağlanması amaçlanıyor. BİLGE sistemindeki teknik düzenlemeler tamamlandı Ticaret Bakanlığı, yeni uygulama kapsamında ihtiyaç duyulan tüm teknik düzenlemelerin BİLGE sisteminde tamamlandığını ve uygulamaya alındığını açıkladı. Yeni sistemle sektör temsilcilerinin gümrük işlemlerini daha hızlı, şeffaf ve etkin şekilde gerçekleştirebilmesi hedefleniyor. Şirketlerin dikkat etmesi gereken kurallar açıklandı Ticaret Bakanlığı, yeni düzenlemenin sorunsuz uygulanabilmesi için firmaların ve gümrük müşavirlerinin dikkat etmesi gereken hususları da sıraladı. Buna göre: - Yetkili kurumlara yapılacak başvuruların ardından firmaların vergi numaralarının sistemle doğru şekilde ilişkilendirilmesi gerekiyor. - Gümrük beyannamelerinde uygun muafiyet kodlarının seçilmesi önem taşıyor. - Belirlenen izin sürelerine uyulması gerekiyor. - Muafiyet kapsamında ithal edilen eşyaların devri, satışı ve kiralanmasında ilgili mevzuata uyulması gerekiyor. - Eşyaların kullanım amacına ilişkin mevzuat hükümlerine uygun hareket edilmesi gerekiyor. Uygulama broşürü de yayımlandı Ticaret Bakanlığı, firmaların ve gümrük müşavirlerinin yeni uygulamayı takip edebilmesi amacıyla bir uygulama broşürü de yayımladı. Bakanlık, ilgili kurumlarla iş birliği içerisinde denizcilik ve havacılık sektörlerinin ihtiyaçlarına yönelik, gümrük işlemlerinde öngörülebilirliği ve etkinliği artıran düzenlemelerin sürdürüleceğini bildirdi.

articles.title: SPK'dan Peker GYO'da Tera kararı! Oy hakları çözülüyor, işlem kısıtı kaldırılıyor
articles.summary: SPK, Tera Portföy Algoritmik Stratejiler Serbest Fon ve Tera Yatırım'ın elindeki Peker GYO payları için yeni karar aldı. 16 Eylül'den bu yana donmuş olan oy hakları çözülecek, payların borsada işlem göremeyen statüsünden çıkarılması için MKK'ya bildirim yapılacak.
articles.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
articles.titleTr: SPK'dan Peker GYO'da Tera kararı! Oy hakları çözülüyor, işlem kısıtı kaldırılıyor
articles.summaryTr: SPK, Tera Portföy Algoritmik Stratejiler Serbest Fon ve Tera Yatırım'ın elindeki Peker GYO payları için yeni karar aldı. 16 Eylül'den bu yana donmuş olan oy hakları çözülecek, payların borsada işlem göremeyen statüsünden çıkarılması için MKK'ya bildirim yapılacak.
articles.articleText: SPK'dan Peker GYO'da Tera kararı! Oy hakları çözülüyor, işlem kısıtı kaldırılıyor - SPK, Tera Portföy Algoritmik Stratejiler Serbest Fon ve Tera Yatırım'ın elindeki Peker GYO payları için yeni karar aldı. 16 Eylül'den bu yana donmuş olan oy hakları çözülecek, payların borsada işlem göremeyen statüsünden çıkarılması için MKK'ya bildirim yapılacak. Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK), Tera Portföy Algoritmik Stratejiler Serbest Fon ile Tera Yatırım Menkul Değerler AŞ'nin elinde bulunan Peker Gayrimenkul Yatırım Ortaklığı (PEKGY) paylarına ilişkin yeni kararını açıkladı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle SPK'nın 19 Kasım 2026 tarihli bülteninde yer alan karara göre, söz konusu payların 16 Eylül 2026 itibarıyla kendiliğinden donmuş olan oy hakları çözülecek. Kurul ayrıca kararın Ticaret Bakanlığı ve Merkezi Kayıt Kuruluşu'na (MKK) bildirilmesine hükmetti. Peker GYO payları yeniden işlem görebilecek mi? SPK'nın kararında, Tera Portföy Algoritmik Stratejiler Serbest Fon ve Tera Yatırım Menkul Değerler AŞ'nin Peker GYO sermayesinde sahip olduğu payların, Borsa İstanbul'da alım satıma konu yapılamayacak paylar statüsünden çıkarılması gerektiğinin MKK'ya bildirilmesi de yer aldı. Böylece söz konusu payların işlem kısıtının kaldırılması yönünde önemli bir adım atılmış oldu. Tera Portföy ve Tera Yatırım için tasfiye süreci SPK, 26 Ekim 2026 tarihli kararıyla Tera Portföy Algoritmik Stratejiler Serbest Fon'un tasfiyesi için Türkiye İş Bankası'nı görevlendirmişti. Kurul, 27 Ekim 2026 tarihinde ise Tera Yatırım Menkul Değerler AŞ'nin tedrici tasfiyesine karar vermişti. Son kararla birlikte tasfiye sürecindeki iki kuruluşun Peker GYO sermayesinde sahip olduğu payların oy hakları ve borsada işlem görebilme statüsü konusunda yeni bir aşamaya geçildi.

articles.titleTr: SPK'dan Midas'a kritik yetki: Meka Global'e (MEKAG) milyonluk ceza!
articles.summaryTr: Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK), 19 Kasım 2026 tarihli bülteninde iki şirketin sermaye artırımı başvurusunu onayladı. Meka Global ve Fibabanka'ya idari para cezası uygulanırken Midas Menkul Değerler'e geniş yetkili aracı kurum olma izni verildi.
articles.articleText: SPK'dan Midas'a kritik yetki: Meka Global'e (MEKAG) milyonluk ceza! - Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK), 19 Kasım 2026 tarihli bülteninde iki şirketin sermaye artırımı başvurusunu onayladı. Meka Global ve Fibabanka'ya idari para cezası uygulanırken Midas Menkul Değerler'e geniş yetkili aracı kurum olma izni verildi. SPK'nın 2026/82 numaralı bülteninde yer alan kararlara göre Kayseri Şeker Tarım Ürünleri Lisanslı Depoculuk AŞ ve Bursa Çimento Fabrikası AŞ'nin sermaye artırımı başvuruları onaylandı. - CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Kayseri Şeker: 30 milyon TL olan mevcut sermayesini 80 milyon TL'ye çıkaracak. 50 milyon TL'lik bedelli sermaye artırımı tahsisli olarak gerçekleştirilecek. - Bursa Çimento: 1,5 milyar TL olan mevcut sermayesini 4,5 milyar TL'ye yükseltecek. Artırımın 1,5 milyar TL'si bedelli, 1,5 milyar TL'si iç kaynaklardan karşılanacak. Bursa Çimento'nun sermaye artırımı halka arz yöntemiyle gerçekleştirilecek. Meka Global'e 3,32 milyon TL ceza SPK, Meka Global Makine İmalat Sanayi ve Ticaret AŞ hakkında yapılan inceleme sonucunda şirkete ve üç kişiye idari para cezası uygulanmasına karar verdi. Cezaların gerekçesi, halka arz gelirlerinin izahnamede belirtilen fon kullanım yeri raporuna uygun kullanılmaması ve bu konudaki raporlama yükümlülüklerinin yerine getirilmemesi oldu. Şirketin ilk genel kurul toplantısında, söz konusu aykırılıkta sorumluluğu bulunan yönetim kurulu üyelerine cezanın rücu edilip edilmeyeceği konusunda karar alınması gerekiyor. Fibabanka'ya 354 bin TL idari para cezası SPK, Fibabanka AŞ'ye de 354.803,96 TL idari para cezası uygulanmasına karar verdi. Cezanın gerekçesi, bankanın 14 Ağustos 2025 tarihli varlığa dayalı menkul kıymet ihracına ilişkin yönetim kurulu kararı hakkında özel durum açıklaması yapmaması oldu. Midas Menkul Değerler'e geniş yetkili aracı kurum izni SPK, Midas Menkul Değerler AŞ'nin portföy aracılığı faaliyet izni alarak geniş yetkili aracı kuruma dönüşme talebini olumlu karşıladı. İzin kapsamında şirket; - Paylar ve diğer menkul kıymetler, - Paya dayalı türev araçlar, - Kaldıraçlı alım satım işlemleri, - Pay endekslerine dayalı türev araçlar, - Diğer türev araçlar alanlarında faaliyet gösterebilecek. Midas, 1,7 milyar TL ve 10 milyon dolarlık ihraç tavanı aldı SPK bülteninde borçlanma aracı ihraçlarına ilişkin onaylar da yer aldı. İhraçlar tahvil ve finansman bonosu kapsamında gerçekleştirilecek. Midas'ın 10 milyon dolarlık ihracı ise yurt dışına yönelik olacak. Inveo Portföy'ün sermaye artırımına izin SPK, Inveo Portföy Yönetimi AŞ'nin 95 milyon TL olan çıkarılmış sermayesinin 170 milyon TL'ye yükseltilmesi talebini de olumlu karşıladı. Böylece şirketin sermayesinde 75 milyon TL'lik artışa izin verilmiş oldu. Peker GYO paylarıyla ilgili karar SPK, Tera Portföy Algoritmik Stratejiler Serbest Fon ve Tera Yatırım Menkul Değerler AŞ'nin Peker Gayrimenkul Yatırım Ortaklığı AŞ sermayesindeki paylarına ilişkin önemli bir karar aldı. Kurul, 16 Eylül 2026 itibarıyla kendiliğinden donmuş olan oy haklarının çözülmesine karar verdi. Ayrıca söz konusu payların Borsa İstanbul'da alım satıma konu yapılamayacak paylar statüsünden çıkarılması için Merkezi Kayıt Kuruluşu'na bildirim yapılmasına hükmedildi.

articles.summaryTr: Belediye başkanı veya başkan vekilliği makamının boşalması halinde yapılacak seçimlere ilişkin yeni kurallar yürürlüğe girdi. Adaylık başvurularına süre sınırı getirilirken birleşik oy pusulası, kapalı kabin ve gözlemci uygulaması zorunlu hale getirildi.
articles.articleText: Resmi Gazete'de yayımlandı: Belediye başkanı seçiminde yeni dönem! İşte yeni kurallar - Belediye başkanı veya başkan vekilliği makamının boşalması halinde yapılacak seçimlere ilişkin yeni kurallar yürürlüğe girdi. Adaylık başvurularına süre sınırı getirilirken birleşik oy pusulası, kapalı kabin ve gözlemci uygulaması zorunlu hale getirildi. Belediye Meclisi Çalışma Yönetmeliği'nde değişiklik yapılmasına ilişkin yönetmelik, 20 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanarak yürürlüğe girdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Çevre, Şehircilik ve İklim Değişikliği Bakanlığı tarafından hazırlanan düzenlemeyle belediye başkanlığı veya başkan vekilliğinin herhangi bir nedenle boşalması durumunda meclis tarafından gerçekleştirilecek seçimlerin usul ve esasları yeniden düzenlendi. Adaylık başvurusu için ilk oturum şartı Yeni düzenlemeye göre belediye başkanlığı veya başkan vekilliği seçimi için aday olmak isteyen belediye meclis üyeleri ile aday göstermek isteyen siyasi parti gruplarının başvurularını, oylama toplantısının ilk birleşiminin ilk oturumunda meclis başkanlık divanına bildirmesi gerekecek. İlk oturumun ardından yeni adaylık başvurusu yapılamayacak. Ancak adaylar her oylama oturumu öncesinde adaylıktan çekilebilecek. Adayların isimleri oylama başlamadan önce meclise duyurulacak ve tutanağa geçirilecek. Seçimler birleşik oy pusulasıyla yapılacak Belediye başkanı ve başkan vekili seçimlerinde birleşik oy pusulası kullanılacak. Oy pusulalarında adayların ad ve soyadları alfabetik sırayla basılı olacak. Meclis üyeleri, tercih ettikleri adayın isminin bulunduğu alana tercih mührü basarak oy kullanacak. Oy pusulaları zarfa konularak şeffaf sandığa atılacak. Oy verme işleminin gizliliğini sağlamak amacıyla en az iki kapalı oy verme kabini hazırlanacak. Seçimlerde gözlemci uygulaması getirildi Düzenlemeyle seçim sürecinin denetlenmesine yönelik yeni bir uygulama da getirildi. Her siyasi parti grubu ile bağımsız üyeler adına, talep edilmesi halinde birer kişi gözlemci olarak görev alabilecek. Gözlemciler, seçimle ilgili itiraz, öneri ve tekliflerini başkanlık divanına iletebilecek. Başkanlık divanı, karar vermeden önce gözlemcilerin görüşlerini dinleyecek ve bunları tutanağa geçirecek. Seçimde aday olan kişiler ise oy kullanabilecek ancak seçim oturumlarını yönetemeyecek ve başkanlık divanında görev alamayacak. Hangi oy pusulaları geçersiz sayılacak? Yönetmelikle oyların geçerliliğine ilişkin kurallar da belirlendi. Aşağıdaki durumlarda oy pusulaları geçersiz sayılacak: - Başkanlık divanının mührünü taşımayan pusulalar. - Üzerinde tanıtıcı işaret bulunan pusulalar. - Birden fazla adaya tercih mührü basılan pusulalar. Buna karşılık pusulaların üretiminden veya basımından kaynaklanan leke, kırışıklık ve basım hataları, tanıtıcı işaret niteliğinde olmadıkları sürece geçersizlik nedeni sayılmayacak. Tercih mührünün adayın alanını ayıran çizgilerin dışına taşması da hangi adayın tercih edildiği açıkça anlaşılıyorsa oyun geçerliliğini etkilemeyecek. Sandıktan fazla oy çıkarsa seçim yenilenecek Sandıktan, oy kullanan meclis üyesi sayısından fazla mühürlü zarf çıkması halinde hiçbir zarf açılmadan ilgili turun seçimi yenilenecek. Sandıktan çıkan mühürsüz zarflar ise açılmadan imha edilmek üzere ayrı bir alanda saklanacak. Mühürlü zarfların sayımı ve açılması işlemi devam edecek. Bu belgeler, dava açma süresinin sonuna kadar veya dava açılması halinde mahkeme kararı kesinleşinceye kadar muhafaza edilecek. Yönetmelik yayımlandığı gün yürürlüğe girdi Belediye Meclisi Çalışma Yönetmeliği'nde yapılan değişiklik, 20 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanmasıyla yürürlüğe girdi. Düzenlemenin hükümlerini Çevre, Şehircilik ve İklim Değişikliği Bakanı yürütecek.

articles.titleTr: Türkiye iki ülkeyle havacılık anlaşması imzaladı: Uçuş hakları artırıldı
articles.summaryTr: Türkiye, Suudi Arabistan ile haftalık tarifeli kargo uçuşu hakkını 14'ten 21'e çıkardı. Singapur ile tarifeli yolcu seferi hakları da artırıldı. Yeni düzenlemelerle iki ülke arasındaki hava ulaşımının güçlendirilmesi hedefleniyor.
articles.articleText: Türkiye iki ülkeyle havacılık anlaşması imzaladı: Uçuş hakları artırıldı - Türkiye, Suudi Arabistan ile haftalık tarifeli kargo uçuşu hakkını 14'ten 21'e çıkardı. Singapur ile tarifeli yolcu seferi hakları da artırıldı. Yeni düzenlemelerle iki ülke arasındaki hava ulaşımının güçlendirilmesi hedefleniyor. Türkiye, Suudi Arabistan ve Singapur ile hava ulaşımı bağlantılarını güçlendirecek yeni mutabakatlara imza attı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanlığı tarafından yapılan açıklamada, Montreal'de düzenlenen Uluslararası Sivil Havacılık Örgütü (ICAO) 7. Dünya Hava Ulaştırma Konferansı kapsamında iki ülkeyle mutabakat zaptlarının imzalandığı bildirildi. Anlaşmalara Türkiye adına Sivil Havacılık Genel Müdürü Kemal Yüksek, Suudi Arabistan adına GACA Başkanı Abdulaziz bin Abdullah Al-Duailej ve Singapur adına CAAS Genel Müdürü Han Kok Juan imza attı. Suudi Arabistan'a kargo uçuşu hakkı 21'e çıkarıldı Türkiye ile Suudi Arabistan arasındaki anlaşma kapsamında haftalık tarifeli kargo uçuşu hakkı 14'ten 21'e yükseltildi. Böylece iki ülke arasındaki haftalık tarifeli kargo seferi kapasitesinde 7 uçuşluk artış sağlandı. Yeni düzenlemenin hava yolu şirketlerine daha fazla operasyonel esneklik sunması hedefleniyor. Singapur ile yolcu uçuşu hakları artırıldı Singapur ile yapılan mutabakat kapsamında ise tarifeli yolcu uçuşu hakları artırıldı. Bakanlık, artışın miktarına ilişkin ayrıntı paylaşmazken düzenlemeyle Türkiye ile Singapur arasındaki hava ulaşımı bağlantılarının ve seyahat seçeneklerinin geliştirilmesinin amaçlandığını bildirdi. Bakanlıktan hava ulaşımı açıklaması Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanlığı açıklamasında, iki mutabakatın hava yolu işletmelerine daha fazla esneklik sağlayacağı vurgulandı. Düzenlemelerin Türkiye'nin uluslararası hava ulaşımı bağlantılarını güçlendirmesi ve iki ülkeyle seyahat imkanlarını geliştirmesi hedefleniyor.
